digest: Startups don't take off by themselves — founders must actively push to get them going, like hand-cranking an early car engine.
Recruit your first users manually and one-by-one; don't wait for them to come to you (Stripe's 'Collison installation' set users up on the spot).
Measure progress by weekly growth rate — small numbers compound (10%/week turns 100 users into millions over two years).
Almost all startups are extremely fragile at first; judge them by their potential if founders do the right things, not by current size — and don't dismiss your own startup.
Find users to recruit by launching untargeted, then seeking more of whoever proves most enthusiastic (Pinterest and design bloggers).
Take extraordinary measures to delight early users — an 'insanely great' experience matters more than a great product, and attentiveness can compensate for a buggy early product.
Over-engaging with early users is also the essential feedback loop that makes the product good.
Start narrow: dominate a deliberately small market to reach critical mass before expanding (Facebook starting at Harvard).

Use unscalable variants suited to your case — assemble hardware yourself ('pulling a Meraki'), consult for a single B2B user, use your software on customers' behalf, or run things manually before automating.
Avoid tactics that don't work: the Big Launch and partnerships with big companies — any strategy that omits sustained early effort is suspect.
Think of a startup idea as a vector: what you'll build plus the unscalable things you'll do to start — which often permanently shape the company's DNA for the better.

direction.conceit: Hand-cranking a stalled early automobile engine — the founder is the crank, and the company only turns over through deliberate manual force until it can run on its own combustion.
direction.motif: A recurring hand-crank-and-flywheel: an ignition arc that starts cold and dark, gains glow and rotation slide by slide, tracking effort converting into momentum.
